title: Transient SNAT affinity after VPC peering route swap causing inter-tenant connection bleed
creator: Asha Patel
description: Production customer reports of cross-tenant TCP connections observed immediately after a scheduled peering route swap. Impacted customers are on Dedicated with peered VPCs; symptoms include stray TCP responses that were accepted by previously unrelated client flows. Root cause analysis points to transient SNAT (connection-tracking) state reuse when the dataplane switches active egress path during route update, combined with asymmetric 5-tuple normalization and a short-lived namespace reconciliation race in the nat table rebind logic. This ticket tracks the immediate mitigation, the code fix, regression tests, and customer communication.
impact_summary: Multiple Dedicated tenants experienced brief cross-tenant TCP flow acceptance during automated peering route swaps — observed window ~30s per event, affecting 3 enterprise customers with strict isolation requirements. Customer-impact level: high (possible data to wrong tenant's connection).
steps_to_reproduce: Provision two Dedicated tenants A and B that share a VPC peering configuration through our peering gateway in the same region
Start a long-lived TCP flow from a client in tenant A to an external endpoint via SNAT through our gateway
Trigger a peering route swap (simulate control-plane promotion: drain old path, swap route table entries to new uplink) while TCP flow remains established
Observe connection-tracking entries on the gateway (conntrack) and whether new inbound packets are attributed to existing SNAT state that was bound to a different tenant namespace
Verify whether packets from tenant B's sockets are intermittently accepted on tenant A's NAT mapping
Reproduce in staging with synthetic traffic and extended logging to capture conntrack hash collisions and namespace rebind order.
root_cause: The nat translation layer uses a shared conntrack hash table with a namespace pointer that is updated asynchronously during peering route swaps. During a route swap the sequence is: create new route, install SNAT rewrite, start draining old path, then remove old namespace pointer. A race condition allowed the old conntrack bucket to be temporarily re-pointed or reused for a new tenant before the previous flow timed out, resulting in 5-tuple collisions being misattributed. Additionally, our normalization step did not include ephemeral port salt tied to tenant ID, lowering entropy for collisions under heavy load.
mitigation_deployed: 2026-02-27 03:12 UTC: Emergency rule added in control-plane to quiesce new SNAT mappings while route swaps are pending (mitigates immediate customer impact)
2026-02-27 03:45 UTC: Rolled forward a conservative conntrack timeout increase for established TCP flows to reduce the chance of immediate reuse
2026-02-27 04:30 UTC: Customer communications sent to the three affected tenants with incident summary and mitigation steps
permanent_fix_plan: Introduce tenant-scoped entropy into conntrack keys (include tenant ID and per-tenant salt) to prevent 5-tuple key collisions across namespaces
Serialise the namespace swap operation so that conntrack buckets are drained and marked immutable before being repointed (two-phase commit style): drain -> mark -> swap -> reclaim
Add unit and integration tests that simulate route swaps under high conntrack load with randomized ephemeral ports
Backfill data-plane metrics for conntrack reuse events and expose alerting on >0 reuse-per-minute during peering maintenance windows
Ship a canary rollout to Dedicated customers with peering enabled and run a 48h soak before broad rollout
implementation_notes:
Proposed code change is in runtime/nat/conntrack_rewrite.go. Key changes:
- Add tenant_salt lookup and include in hash input
- Introduce 'drain_marker' flag on buckets to make entries read-only during swap
- Rework namespace unbind path to defer reclaim until no active handles
PR drafted: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12867
